judge_notes.opus: F won by leading with the day's biggest story and giving it stakes: 'Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO after reports of affairs with a suspected Chinese spy ... and its market value fell below $4 trillion,' in tight, complete sentences; its only real weakness is a 'while'-joined closing list. L lost because its lead is vague and hedged ('a new private-law challenge to frontier-model development, though the requested injunction is not a court ruling'), it reduces Claude Meetings to 'a meeting participant that drafts artifacts,' and it omits the Nvidia CEO exit entirely.
judge_notes.astra: J wins narrowly: "days before its November 17 earnings report" gives the leadership change immediate executive relevance and establishes a useful hierarchy. Its benchmark-heavy ending prevents a higher score. S finishes last because "introducing a fourth xhigh thinking tier that reaches 54 on Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index v5" exemplifies its sustained specification overload; every sentence is long, and "Meanwhile" ushers in yet another multi-company inventory. No entry is publication-ready as-is.
judge_notes.grok: R won because each item is its own short, specific sentence — "825 million Class A shares," a named court, an injunction scope — and the only seam is "Separately." S lost because the products stay unnamed functions ("two security-agent products," "a Claude Meetings beta for teams") and the closer is a disclaimer, "the filing is a lawsuit, not a ruling."
judge_notes.dsflash: Best (J) won on hygiene rather than ambition: three clean sentences, no grammar flaw, and each story given its own space — "a speed-first model the company says finishes tasks 2.5x faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash" then "Anthropic set its IPO price range at $70 to $78 per share ahead of a November 19 Nasdaq listing" — with only a tacked-on "with four selectable thinking levels" and a three-story closing paragraph against it. I and R tie just behind: I paragraphs one story at a time and explains the product ("joins Google Meet calls and drafts documents during the meeting") but spends its opening on "$1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens"; R has the same explanatory instinct ("builds documents and whiteboards during the conversation") but buries two stories in a 55-word first sentence. Worst (P) lost on substance: it opens with an abstraction, "a new private-law challenge to frontier-model development", hedges immediately ("the requested injunction is not a court ruling"), and describes everything vaguely — "a meeting participant that drafts artifacts during calls" — with no number, name or claim a reader can use. D and M were the other failures: both run to roughly 190 words, D opening with a ~70-word sentence of pricing and index scores and M with a 65-word sentence ending "2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash", then closing on five-item lists. Between them, H and N carry garbled names ("SpaceXSI") that any copy desk would stop on, and A's "In corporate leadership and product news" is a list header standing in for a point of view.
